title: Exact per-turn Prize trace, the event's round rule as an engine option, and the ending-label fix, validated against #139's end-count proxy
rivals: R1 proxy-faithful: the Prize count at the game's end stands in fairly for the count at the cut, so #139's greedy STS numbers stand (walls 0.64-0.68 of the points at cuts 40-60 over all 24 lists)
R2 late lead: the walls build their Prize lead after the cut, so the exact count lowers their greedy share, most at short cuts
R3 early lead: the walls lead early and the lists catch up late, so the exact count raises their share
design: (1) Trace: env/runner.js and notes/scripts/walls_vs_humans.js rows log, per game turn (both players' turns, as env/game.js counts), each seat's Prizes taken, cards left in deck, attack available, attacked, Trainers played. (2) Ending label: env/game.js records the reason when the win happens (six Prizes, cannot draw, no Pokemon in play), keeping the old label as ending_legacy (#139: a no-Pokemon win against an empty deck is labelled deck-out). (3) Round rule, off by default: --round-rule T through env/game.js, env/runner.js, env/remote_worker.js and rl/metagame.py; when game turn T+1 begins, more Prizes taken wins (time-win), equal is a time-tie; with the rule on, the 5,000-decision cap is decided the same way. Deck scores 1 / 2/3 / 1/3 / 0; per-seat pilot points +1 / +1/3 / -1/3 / -1 (a time loss pays like a loss). Clones carry the rule (search lines crossing T end under it); plain-draw --max-turns stays for comparison. (4) Tests: scripted states at turn T with Prizes 2-1 and 1-1; 20 seeded games with the rule off match the untimed engine move for move (trace hash). (5) Validation: replay #139/#141's greedy all-24 probe (scr-resetcap 499 walls vs the 24 lists, seed 11, stride 32; 576 games in runs/probe/wvh_greedy_all24_g0-7.jsonl, plus g8-15 for 1,152) with the trace; check winners, endings, turns and steps against stored rows; compute the walls' STS share at T in {20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60} exactly and with the proxy on the same games.

predictions.predicted: exact minus proxy within +/-0.02 at every T; the side ahead at the cut is ahead at the end in >= 85% of unfinished games
exact share >= 0.05 below the proxy at T <= 40 (proxy 0.64-0.66 there, so <= 0.60), the gap shrinking toward T 60; walls that later win by deck-out often trail or tie at the cut
exact share >= 0.05 above the proxy at T <= 40

readout: The walls' share of STS points (#139's definition) at each T, exact vs proxy, paired on identical games; how often the side ahead at T wins, by ending and T; replay determinism (share of games identical to stored rows).
noise_and_power: Paired on identical deterministic greedy games: per-game differences move in steps of 1/3 (SD about 0.4), SE about 0.017 at 576 games and 0.012 at 1,152, so 0.05 is 3-4 SE. Determinism checked game by game against 576 stored rows.
kill_rule: If > 0.5% of replayed games differ from the stored rows, or any of the 20 rule-off games diverges from the untimed engine, stop and fix before any evaluation.
cost: About 3-4 h of code and tests (trace 1 h; rule, label and cap 1.5 h; metagame scoring and seat rewards 1 h). Validation replay 5-10 min CPU (576 greedy games took 4.6 min). No screen slot.
distinct_from: H03 and #139/#147 re-scored stored rows with the end-of-game count or a plain draw; no run recorded the count at the cut. These are new traced replays, so H03's do-not-repeat ('re-scoring #139/#147 games at other cuts') holds; the never-varied factor is the exact count. H04 built only a plain draw (#140); H01 left the decision cap paying the pilot 0, better than a loss (removed when the rule is on). The ending-label bug sits unfixed in #139's Next and the critic's list.
rules_check: Evaluation infrastructure: turns, results and the game's own end score only (rule 2); carries to MTG as the reference event's round rule (five extra turns, then a draw). Building it needs no approval; switching it on in training is Evan's decision (C33).
value: Unblocks C13, C14, C15, C16, C31 and C34 and settles the one local fact against the round rule (#139: greedy walls still take 0.63-0.68 of STS points). R2: the clock helps even under the greedy population judge; R1/R3: it needs search-strength play, so a training-side test (C34) runs only with a search judge.

reviews.reasons:
On paper the rivals separate cleanly. R1 predicts a gap within ±0.02, R2 a gap of at least -0.05 and R3 at least +0.05. The readout is paired on identical deterministic games and sits on the right node (N12 measurement), and 0.05 is about 3-4 SE. The diagnostic half of the candidate, though, has already been run, and its "never measured" premise is false.

The Prize trace already exists. notes/scripts/walls_vs_humans.js writes a per-turn prizeTrace (log #150), walls_vs_humans_report.py scores the STS rule from it exactly, and runs/probe/sts_exact_chain.sh has already replayed the all-24 greedy probe (runs/probe/sts_greedy_all24.jsonl) plus two search runs on 8 human lists. I re-scored that file against the stored rows in runs/probe/wvh_greedy_all24_g0-7.jsonl:
- **Determinism:** 576 of 576 games match on winner, ending, turns, steps and Prizes left.
- **Exact vs proxy** (#139's 3/2/1 points):

| Turn cut | Proxy | Exact |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 0.657 | 0.482 |
| 25 | 0.654 | 0.515 |
| 30 | 0.650 | 0.543 |
| 35 | 0.646 | 0.547 |
| 40 | 0.641 | 0.553 |
| 45 | 0.644 | 0.588 |
| 50 | 0.655 | 0.620 |
| 60 | 0.675 | 0.665 |

- **Lead at the cut vs lead at the end:** in unfinished games the side ahead at the cut is the side ahead at the end in only 53-82% of them (cuts 20-60).

So R2 (late lead) is clearly supported and R1 and R3 are refuted. Step 5 would only re-confirm a known result and is now on H03's do-not-repeat list. The distinct_from claim that "no run recorded the count at the cut" is wrong.

What is left is real infrastructure value:
- the round rule as an engine and metagame option;
- the ending-label fix;
- the extra trace fields (cards left in deck, attack available, attacked, Trainers played);
- seat rewards under the rule.

For these, the validation and the decision value have to be restated:
- The 0.5% replay tolerance is too loose for a deterministic engine that already replays at 0%.
- The SE assumes independent games, but the games cluster as 72 wall-list pairs of 8 games each.
- The candidate's points scheme (1 / 2/3 / 1/3 / 0, so a time-tie pays 1/3 to each side) must match the report's (3/0, time-win 2/0, tie 1/1). Otherwise engine-scored and offline numbers will not line up.
- The value statement now needs to follow from R2: under the greedy judge, the rule at cuts of 30-45 still leaves the walls above 0.5 (0.54-0.59). The rule alone probably does not flip the judge, and that is the prediction C34 has to pre-register.

R2 is supported, and lead sign at the cut matches the end in 53-82% of unfinished games. Change the validation of the engine round rule. With the rule on at T in {30, 40, 50}, the engine's result for each game in sts_greedy_all24's deals must equal the offline prizeTrace scoring of the same game, with zero mismatches allowed. With the rule off, the replay must match stored rows 576/576.

Make one points scheme consistent across the engine, rl/metagame.py and walls_vs_humans_report.py (report: 3/0, time-win 2/0, Prize tie 1/1). State how the deck score and per-seat pilot reward map onto it, including that a time-tie is not zero-sum.
For the ending-label fix, pre-state and report how many of the probe's 148 + 27 deck-out labels and 23 + 42 no-Pokemon labels change.

Rewrite value and rules_check for the R2 outcome. Under the greedy judge the rule cuts the walls' share, but they stay above 0.5 at T 30-60 (0.54-0.67) and drop below it only at a cut of about 20. reviews.reasons:
Rules: no violation. The trace, the ending label and an off-by-default round rule are evaluation and engine infrastructure. They use only turns, results and the game's own Prize score, and they carry to MTG as an event's round rule. The candidate correctly leaves switching the rule on in training to Evan (C33). Note that when Evan was asked about the 2000 round rule in #140, he asked only for a plain draw limit, so a Prize tiebreak in training stays gated on him.

Feasibility: the cost is overstated, and the validation half is largely redundant with work that already exists in the repo.
(a) notes/scripts/walls_vs_humans.js already records a per-turn Prize trace (`prizeTrace`, log #150; Prizes left as each turn begins, both seats).
(b) notes/scripts/walls_vs_humans_report.py already has `sts_points()`, which scores the STS rule exactly at any cut.
(c) runs/probe/sts_exact_chain.sh has already replayed the #139/#141 greedy all-24 probe with the trace (runs/probe/sts_greedy_all24.jsonl, 576 games). It also replayed the search-on-human subset (sts_search_human_sub.jsonl, 192 games) and was partway through the search-both subset (sts_search_both_sub.jsonl, 148 of 192 games when the log was last written).
So the claim "no run recorded the count at the cut" is false. Step (5) can also be computed from stored rows in seconds, with no replay.

I ran that check (scratch script C:/Users/evanc/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-evanc-Desktop-333/9afecfab-fdea-4a82-8aad-02daab001fd1/scratchpad/c01_check.py):
- Determinism: 0 of 576 traced games differ from the stored wvh_greedy_all24_g0-7 rows in winner, ending, turns, steps or Prizes left.
- Walls' STS share, exact vs proxy, on identical games:

| Cut T | Exact | Proxy |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 0.482 | 0.657 |
| 25 | 0.515 | 0.654 |
| 30 | 0.543 | 0.650 |
| 35 | 0.547 | 0.646 |
| 40 | 0.553 | 0.641 |
| 45 | 0.588 | 0.644 |
| 50 | 0.620 | 0.655 |
| 60 | 0.665 | 0.675 |

So R2 (late lead) is already confirmed by about 0.09-0.18 at T 20-40, the gap shrinking toward T 60, and R1 and R3 are refuted. The proxy overstated the walls under the greedy judge. #139's greedy figure of 0.63-0.68 does not stand at short cuts.

The engineering that remains is real and modest:
- The round rule with the Prize decision in env/game.js. The existing `maxTurns`/`timedOut`/`winner`/`ending`/`clone` path is the template, and the 5,000-decision `MAX_STEPS` cap is decided the same way.
- Plumbing through env/env.js, runner.js, remote_worker.js (`games`, `tsearch` and the training-games command that takes `maxTurns`) and rl/metagame.py.
- Extending the trace fields (cards in deck, attack available, attacked, Trainers played) and moving the trace into runner.js.
- The ending-label fix.

About 2-3 h. No screen slot is needed.

Hidden costs and risks the design does not cover:
- runner.js:76 and remote_worker.js:412 pay `deckoutWin` on `ending === 'deck-out'`, so relabelling changes training rewards for any run with `--deckout-win` other than 1. The reward path must stay pinned to `ending_legacy`, or the change has to be logged as a reward change.
- STS deck scoring 1 / 2/3 / 1/3 / 0 is not constant-sum: a time-tie pays 2/3 in total. rl/metagame.py treats a draw as 0.5 to each deck. `judged()`, the selection bars and any symmetric-matrix assumption need checking before the rule is used in the population.
- The pilot payoffs +1 / +1/3 / -1/3 / -1 are not zero-sum for a time-tie in shared-pilot PPO. That is acceptable, but it should be stated.
- Search agents (psearch in walls_vs_humans.js and env/agents.js, tsearch) score a clone's terminal `winner` as 0 at a time-out. Under the rule they must read the Prize decision, or search will misvalue lines that cross T.
- Adding a per-turn trace to runner.js rows for 2,000 population games an iteration adds IPC volume, so it should be opt-in.
- The ending-label fix needs the engine's actual loss trigger: deck-out at the draw step vs no Pokemon after a KO. Reordering checks in the `ending` getter is not enough.
- g8-15 has no stored rows, so those 576 games are new games, not a replay check (about 4.5 min CPU).

title: Outside research on the specification: STS 2000 round rule, engine turns per 20-minute round, human game length, how stall decks fared, 2000 procedure rules, Phase B and C event rules
rivals: R-fast / clock binds: 20 minutes allowed about 20-50 engine turns, time was called often, deck-outs were rare and stall decks lost on Prizes at time; the human meta is optimal only under the clock
R-slow / clock slack: rounds allowed 60-70+ engine turns or rarely reached time, and stall decks were weak for other reasons (Haymaker's speed, Gust of Wind); the clock is not the lever
H-pilot-slow: human games ended far faster than our pilots' (the lists' Prize wins take 34-41 engine turns here, 46-47 against the walls greedy), so P's tempo deficit is large in absolute terms
R-unknown: no quantitative evidence survives; T must come from a stated prior or the game's own self-play length
design: Time-boxed web research (about 4 h, deep-research workflow; every quote re-checked by a second agent). Q1 STS California, 22 July 2000 (Long Beach): round length per age division (15+, 11-14, 10 and under), procedure at time (stop, finish the turn, extra turns), points (win 3, time win 2, Prize tie 1, loss 0), one game per Swiss round, rounds and top cut, top-cut games at time, slow play. Sources: old.pokemonaaah.net/other/junk/sts/fossil.shtml (#139's verifier), pokemontcgarchive.wordpress.com, Wizards of the Coast 1999-2000 tournament, floor and League rules (archive.org), Pojo. Q2 Engine turns (both players') per 20-minute round in Base-Jungle-Fossil-Rocket play; share of rounds reaching time and games ending by deck-out; turns per player to take six Prizes with Haymaker or Wigglytuff (reports with turn counts or 'time was called', 2000 speed articles, timestamped retro recordings; modern data as an anchor only). Q3 Were Chansey/Snorlax walls with Potion Energy, Full Heal Energy, Energy Removal and Gambler (healing Energy new with Team Rocket), or other stall decks (Mr. Mime, Energy denial), played April-November 2000, and called weak because of time or for other reasons? (Pojo/PokeGym, other 2000 lists, the repo's STS New Jersey lists: November, Gym-legal, Chansey only as a tech.) Q4 2000 procedure rules: first-turn draw, attack and Trainers; mulligans (the engine gives the opponent 1 optional card per mulligan); Confusion (engine follows 2003); simultaneous wins and Sudden Death; when a deck-out loss happens (Base-Rocket rulebooks, 1999-2000 Compendium). Q5 Phase B and C rules fixed before any run: Worlds 2005 (games per match, round length, extra turns, unfinished matches) and the Magic Tournament Rules (50 minutes, five extra turns, then a draw; 3/1/0). Q6 Active era-format communities or archives of recorded games (TCG ONE, ryuu.eu, Discord leagues) for Q2's lengths or a live evaluation (human data, evaluation only). Q7 Did the three age divisions share rules, and are the 24 lists each division's top 8?

predictions.predicted: Q2: about 10-25 turns per player per round (20-50 engine turns), about 10-12 per player to take six Prizes, reports of rounds ending at time; T prior <= 50; Q3: stall decks rare or described as losing on time
Q2: 60-70+ engine turns per round or rounds rarely reaching time; Q3: stall decks played and beaten by speed, not time; T prior 70+ or 'rarely binding'
human Haymaker and Wigglytuff wins in about 6-10 own turns (12-20 engine turns), about half our pilots' 34-41
fewer than two independent sources for Q2; C13's stated prior stays the decision of record and the whole T curve is reported

readout: A table per question: answer, quotes and URLs, number of independent sources, confidence, and the decision it feeds (the rule's form in C01; the T interval for C13, C31, C34; fidelity checks for C06; Phase B/C rules and the answer key's scope for C33); a human game-length yardstick.
noise_and_power: Evidence quality, not sampling: primary rule documents outrank player reports; a number needs >= 2 independent primary sources and is reported as a range. One authoritative document settles Q1, Q4 or Q5; Q2 needs about 10 reported games with turn counts or 3 timed recordings.
kill_rule: Stop at the 4-hour box; drop a question after 45 min without a primary source and record it as unknown (then use C13's whole T curve). Never use outside data on which decks won to set any training parameter.
cost: About 4 h of agent time plus a fact-check pass; no GPU or CPU contention.
distinct_from: H03's untested '[outside research] turns per 20-minute STS 2000 round; did players avoid stall decks' and H61's untested 'era players or transcribed 2000-era games' were never run; #144 and the 11-angle survey covered RL literature and other games' rule texts, not this event or the 2000 procedure rules (the degenerate-env angle found only the STS page, silent on extra turns). #139 used an unknown cut and #147's T 50-60 was read after seeing where the verdict flips. The critic's one 'purely external blocker'.
rules_check: Facts defining the environment (like the card pool and the 60-card rule) are not decklists, bots or shaping; they enter only as the rule's parameters, fixed before any run; T never comes from its effect on distance to the human lists (autobalancing); Q6 human data is evaluation only. Adopting the clock in training is Evan's decision (C33).
value: Supplies the clock's one parameter, T, without fitting the answer key; tests the premise (were the walls kept out by the clock?); fixes Phase B and C rules in advance; turns 'the pilot plays tempo decks slowly' into a measurable target. Analysis section 7's premise-check trigger.

reviews.reasons:
Not a repeat. The candidate is distinct on node (N1 game definition and N12 measurement) and on mechanism: it is outside research on the event's specification, not another run, re-score or screen. No family has run it.

Ledger overlap, checked against the full ledger_digest:
- **H03** (the walls' edge is the long, clockless game) lists "[outside research] Turns per 20-minute STS 2000 round; did players avoid stall decks" as untested. Its verifier says #139 calls the engine-turn equivalent "unknown".
- **H61** lists "[outside research] Era players or transcribed 2000-era games" as untested. Grep found no hits.
- The do-not-repeat lists for H03, H51 and the turn-limit families block these, and the candidate does none of them: re-scoring the #139/#147 games at other cuts, plain-draw `--max-turns` at 40, 70 or 120, `--gamma 0.995`, `--deckout-win 0`, greedy judging with a 60-turn limit, and the judge sweeps. It uses no GPU or CPU and changes no training parameter.
- The degenerate-env research angle concludes that "the next step is a research step on the specification, not another screen". It names exactly these missing facts: the event's exact rules, how many turns a 2000-era 20-minute game ran, and the Worlds 2005 and MTG event rules.

Progress-log grep:
- #139 quoted only the archived STS page: 20-minute Swiss rounds, a time win worth 2 of 3 points, a Prize tie worth 1 each. It states "how many engine turns 20 minutes allowed is unknown".
- #140's turn limit was a plain draw chosen by Evan's request 24. Nothing in the log looked for human game lengths, timed recordings, or how stall decks fared in 2000.

The factor never varied before is outside evidence for T and for the premise that "the clock kept the walls out", gathered before any run. This answers the fact-check objection that #147's T of 50-60 was read after seeing where the verdict flips.

Partial overlaps should be trimmed so the 4-hour box is not spent re-finding known facts. They do not warrant a revise.
1. **Q1:** the round length and the 3/2/1/0 points are already quoted from old.pokemonaaah.net (#139 verifier). Re-check only the age divisions, the procedure at time, top-cut games at time and slow play.
2. **Q4:** notes/sts-2000-engine-check.md already ran the 2000-era Compendium rulings (22/23 pass, T18 the one failure). #139 already listed the known engine deviations: Confusion follows the 2003 rule, a simultaneous win is a draw with no Sudden Death, and the deck-out label issue. Q4 should start from those and ask only what they leave open: first-turn draw, attack and Trainers, the mulligan bonus, and when a deck-out loss happens.
3. **Q5:** MTR 2.4 (five additional turns, then a draw) is already sourced in research_notes/degenerate-env.md, so only the Worlds 2005 match rules are new.

The rules check holds. Environment facts enter only as the rule's parameters, fixed in advance. Deck-success data must not set training parameters. Adopting the clock stays Evan's decision (request 24 chose a plain draw, so the Prize-tiebreak rule still needs his go-ahead).
required_changes: Before searching, seed Q1, Q4 and Q5 from what the repo already holds: the STS page quote in #139, notes/sts-2000-engine-check.md (Compendium rulings, 22/23) and the MTR 2.4 citations in research_notes/degenerate-env.md. Spend the time box only on the facts still unknown, mainly Q2, Q3, Q6, the age-division and top-cut details in Q1/Q7, and the Worlds 2005 match rules.

Write the decision rule from Q2's answer to a T interval (or 'unknown', which means C13's whole T curve) into the readout before the research starts, so T cannot be chosen after looking at where the #147 verdict flips.
Record the outcome as a tried row for H03's and H61's outside-research variants in the ledger and in notes/evan-requests.md (rows 24 and 33), so it is not proposed again.

reviews.reasons:
Diagnosticity is adequate on the main readout. Q1 and Q2 produce numbers (minutes per round, procedure at time, engine turns per round, how often rounds reached time) on which R-fast (T <= 50, time often called) and R-slow (T 70+, time rarely reached) predict different values. R-unknown is a legitimate outcome that still feeds a decision: C13 then reports the whole T curve. The readout matches the targeted nodes. N1 and N12 are about how the game and the measurement are defined, and a table of documented rules and game lengths is the right instrument for that. A deck-shape or Elo readout would be wrong here, and the candidate correctly avoids one. Sampling noise is not the issue. The source-quality rules are sensible: primary documents outrank player reports, a number needs at least 2 independent primary sources and is reported as a range, and a second agent re-checks every quote. The kill rules (a 4-hour box, 45 minutes per question) suit time-boxed research, and short-horizon bias does not apply. The rules check is sound: environment facts enter only as parameters fixed in advance, nothing is fitted to the answer key, and Q6 human data is used for evaluation only. The cost is low with no GPU contention, and the analysis's section 7 premise-check trigger applies directly.

There are four weaknesses.
(1) Q3 does not discriminate as written. Both R-fast and R-slow predict that walls were rare at STS 2000, so "rare" settles nothing. The two rivals differ only in why the walls lost. Player-stated reasons are anecdotal and confounded by availability: the healing Energy was new with Team Rocket.
(2) H-pilot-slow is not a rival to R-fast and R-slow. It is a separate axis, and it can be true under either clock hypothesis. Its comparison also mixes units and conditioning. "6-10 own turns" in human reports would be compared with our 34-41 engine turns, which count only Prize wins between the lists. Human reports are also selected toward memorable, quick wins.
(3) The plan has no conversion fixed in advance from evidence to T. #147's T 50-60 was read after seeing where the verdict flips, so the same risk applies here unless the mapping is written down before any source is read. Recordings from online clients (TCG ONE) and modern retro play have a different pace per turn than 2000 in-person play, with physical shuffling, setup and young divisions.
(4) The budget is spread thin. Seven questions in 4 hours leaves about 34 minutes each, which conflicts with the 45-minute drop rule. Q5 (Phase B and C) and Q7 do not feed T or the premise check.

One readout already in hand is a free discriminator and should be used: our engine ends 27-35% of human-list-vs-human-list games by deck-out (JF2). R-fast and H-pilot-slow both predict that human deck-outs were rare. A documented human deck-out rate is therefore directly comparable to ours, with no conversion of units.
required_changes: Before reading any source, write down the formula from evidence to T, for example T = (round seconds - setup and shuffle overhead) / (seconds per engine turn), as a range. State the overhead allowances and the rule for combining sources. Also state, in advance, how the T interval maps onto the downstream decisions (C13, C31, C34) and that the mapping will not be revised after seeing results.

Express all game lengths in one unit, engine turns (both players' turns), and record which division a source covers (15+, 11-14, 10 and under). Weight 2000 in-person sources above online-client and modern retro recordings, which serve only as anchors with a stated adjustment for pace.

Recast H-pilot-slow as a separate axis, not a rival to the clock hypotheses. Make the comparison matched: human turns to six Prizes for a named matchup (for example Haymaker mirror or Haymaker vs Wigglytuff) against our pilot's engine turns for the same pair of lists. Condition both sides the same way (Prize wins only, median and range) and note the selection bias in human reports toward memorable, quick wins.

Add a human deck-out rate (share of games ending by deck-out) as a direct readout to compare with JF2's 27-35% in our engine. R-fast and H-pilot-slow predict it was rare. Treat 'no deck-outs reported' as weak evidence unless a source counts games.

Make Q3 discriminating or demote it. Accept as evidence only records of walls or stall decks at a time-called round (results at time, whether they lost on Prizes when time was called) versus losing before time. Record 'stall decks were rare' as non-discriminating, because both R-fast and R-slow predict it, and record that the healing Energy only became legal with Team Rocket.

Reorder the budget. Q1 and Q2 (with the deck-out rate) come first, with at least 2 h between them. Q4 comes next, then Q3. Q5, Q6 and Q7 get only leftover time and must not delay the T decision. Keep the 45-minute drop rule, and log every unanswered question as 'unknown' with what was searched.

reviews.reasons:
Rules: passes. Q1, Q4 and Q5 ask for facts that define the environment: the round clock, the procedure rules and the Phase B/C event rules. Those are the same kind of input as the card pool and the 60-card rule. They are not decklists, bots or game-specific reward shaping. A round clock also carries over to MTG (the MTR gives 50 minutes plus 5 extra turns), so the rule's form is game-agnostic and only its parameter is per game. Q6 human data is evaluation only. The kill rule already forbids using outside data on which decks won to set any training parameter, and adopting the clock is left to Evan (C33). One rules risk remains. Q3 (how stall decks fared) is metagame-outcome information. If it is read before T is fixed, choosing T or choosing to adopt the clock becomes a soft form of autobalancing toward the answer key. That needs an ordering guard (see required changes).

Feasibility: no GPU or CPU contention, so it runs beside the 3 screens at no cost to the machine budget. The engine already supports a clock: env/game.js has maxTurns, which counts both players' turns and ends a game as a draw at turn T+1. It is plumbed through runner.js and remote_worker.js, and metagame.py passes args.max_turns at line 549. So "engine turns per round" maps straight onto the existing parameter, and adopting T needs no engineering. One downstream catch: if Q1 finds that the 2000 time procedure awarded a "time win" on Prizes (the candidate's own 3/2/1/0 points), the current draw-at-cap is the wrong rule form. C01 would need a small engine change in game.js (Prize-count tiebreak at the cap, possibly extra turns). That cost belongs to C01/C33, but this readout should flag it.

Cost: 4 h of research is realistic, but the second-agent re-check of every quote adds about 1 h, so call it about 5 h. Q2 (about 10 reported 2000-era games with turn counts, or 3 timed recordings) is the weakest question. R-unknown is the likely outcome, and the 45-minute drop rule handles that correctly by falling back to C13's whole T curve. The deep-research workflow needs a subagent-spawning tool. This reviewer session has none, so the main loop must run it.
required_changes: Pre-register the ordering. Derive the T interval (or 'unknown') only from Q1/Q2/Q4 (rule documents and game-length evidence) and record it before Q3's answer on how stall decks fared is read or reported to the decision-maker. Q3 feeds only the premise diagnosis (were walls kept out by the clock?), never T, the rule's form or the decision to adopt the clock.

Revise the cost to about 5 h of agent time (4 h research plus about 1 h for the second-agent quote re-check). State that the main loop runs the deep-research workflow, since it needs a subagent-spawning tool.

In the Q1 readout, state which time-call procedure applied (draw, Prize-count time win, extra turns). Note that the existing engine cap (env/game.js maxTurns) scores every unfinished game as a draw, so a Prize tiebreak or extra-turns rule needs a small game.js change, costed in C01/C33.

Q6 is identification only: list communities and archives and pull public recorded games. Contact no players and start no live evaluation without Evan's approval. All human game data stays evaluation and diagnosis only.

title: GPU-served searched probe with common random numbers: parity with #147's CPU result, and whether half of what one-turn search changes is re-deal noise
rivals: Same-judge: the learner-served search used in the loop (rl/remote.py top-k, env/remote_worker.js RemotePilot, 40-step lines, PyTorch not ONNX) is the judge #139/#147 measured on CPU
Different-judge: the in-loop path differs (step cap, top-k ties, numerics), so scr-jsearch479 searched with an unvalidated judge

Re-deal noise: psearch and tsearch re-deal hidden cards independently per option (env/agents.js:377-380; tsearch a seed per line), so much of search's 50-54% departure from the pilot's top option (#149) and of the expert-iteration targets' 60-70% disagreement (#103-106) is deal luck
CRN-null / signal: searched choices are stable under re-deals; the leaf value or rollout policy limits search
design: Code: notes/scripts/probe_searched.py sends the metagame 'games' message with fixed deck lists and gpu_matrix deal seeds (#137/#147 deals); every job flagged search with judgeSearch {k, dets, maxSteps 40}, optional maxTurns or C01's rule, per-seat search, the learner serving slot 0; one JSONL row per game (winner, ending, turns, per-turn Prizes from C01, searches, changed, lines, capped). A crn option in PolicySearchAgent and tsearch (one seed per determinization shared by all options), passed through judgeSearch. Tests (env/tools/test_search.js): k 1 replays the greedy game exactly; identical options score identically under CRN. Validation A, games: #147's 192 deals (8 lists, one per archetype, x 3 walls x 8), resetcap499 pilot, both seats searched: (a) independent k4 d4, (b) CRN k4 d4, (c) CRN k8 d2; extend to all 576 deals if (a) and (b) differ by 0.03-0.08. Validation B, positions: 2,000 main-phase positions from population games (human-free) and 500 from human-vs-human games (evaluation), each configuration run twice with independent master seeds: k4 d4 independent, k4 d4 CRN, k8 d2 CRN, k16 d1 (16 lines a decision, horizon 1); self-agreement, off-top-option rate, C10's per-class puzzles.

predictions.predicted: (a) scores 0.573 +/- 0.07 (#147 on CPU) with a changed share of 0.50-0.56, as in scr-jsearch479's rows (0.50-0.54)
(a) off 0.573 by > 0.10, or its changed share outside 0.45-0.60: debug before any searched result is used, scr-jsearch479's included

independent k4d4 self-agreement <= 0.65 on positions with >= 3 options, CRN raising it to >= 0.80; off-top rate down >= 25% (about 0.5 to <= 0.38); (b) moves the walls' score >= 0.03 (downward expected); puzzles within +/-2 points; k8 d2 CRN matches or beats k4 d4 at equal lines
independent self-agreement already >= 0.80; CRN changes the off-top rate < 10% (changed share < 0.05), the score < 0.03 and puzzles < 2 points

readout: Searched verdict on walls vs lists (evaluation) and paired differences across (a)-(c); changed / off-top share; self-agreement; line errors and capped lines; seconds per searched game; per-class puzzles; population and human-vs-human positions separately.
noise_and_power: Each 192-game arm +/-0.07; paired across arms SE about 0.04 (shifts above about 0.08 resolve at 192 games, 0.05 at 576). The changed share rests on about 20,000 searched decisions (SE < 0.005); 2,000 positions give agreement and off-top SE about 0.01, so 0.05 is > 4 SE.
kill_rule: If (a) differs from 0.573 by > 0.10, stop and debug before the path is used anywhere. If independent self-agreement is >= 0.85, keep the current search. Drop CRN if it raises agreement < 0.05 and moves neither the changed share by 0.05 nor the score by 0.03. Drop (c) if its line errors exceed 1%.
cost: About 3-4 h of code (reuses rl/metagame.py dispatch and rl/remote.py; CRN is 10-20 lines in env/agents.js and env/remote_worker.js) plus tests. Compute: 3 x 192 searched games at about 1.6 s a game with 4 workers (CPU ONNX about 23 s), 15-20 GPU-min; positions 256k lines, about 10 min (#106: 17,876 lines in 29 s). No screen slot.
distinct_from: #139 and #145-147 ran CPU-ONNX psearch k4 d4 with independent re-deals (H22 do-not-repeat); that setting reruns only to validate a new path. scr-jsearch479 used the GPU path unvalidated (analysis section 9). Shared worlds across options, k8 d2 at equal lines and 8-16 determinizations at k 8 were never run (H22 untested; search-value idea 2); the expert-iteration post-mortems never named independent re-deals (H11); only k 4/8 and horizons 1/2 were varied (#96, #147; H05).
rules_check: Play-time search over legal options with seeded clones; CRN needs only an engine that clones or seeds (MTG engines included). No human data reaches training; the lists are evaluation probes.
value: A searched game about 14x cheaper, paired with a greedy replay of the same deal, which C12, C13, C16, C20 and C38 need; settles whether the in-loop searched judge is the one #147 measured; decides whether CRN enters the judge's search and EI v4's targets (C37 is gated on self-agreement >= 0.80). CRN-null points at the leaf value (C12).
merged_from: judge: GPU-served searched-judge probe with common random numbers, validated against #147's CPU result; pilot: Common random numbers in search: is half of what one-turn search changes just re-deal noise?; chain: step 0 of 'P x E oracle swap on the evaluation game' (GPU-served searched probe, CRN)

reviews.reasons: Distinct by a never-varied factor (common random numbers across options) and by node N12/N4 path validation, not a rerun. The overlapping families are H05, H11, H22, H23, H19 and H62, and their do-not-repeat lists cover only independently re-dealt psearch: k4 dets4 at h1/h2 on #139's 192 deals (H05, H19, H22); hard-argmax EI with 2-4 lines (H11); and --judge-search 200 under the min rule (H23). I checked the code: env/agents.js:378-380 draws a fresh seed per (option, copy) with `new Rng(this.rng.u32())`, and research_notes/search-value.md confirms tsearch does the same per option and line. The progress log mentions common random numbers only for lab forks (#83, and H62's untested 'paired-fork CRN'), never inside search. So CRN in search was never built or varied, and the claim that 'the EI post-mortems never named independent re-deals' holds: #105-106 say only 'targets near noise'. Arm (a), independent k4 d4 on #147's 192 deals with the resetcap499 pilot and both seats searched, is formally the H22 do-not-repeat configuration. Here it is a parity control for a new compute path (GPU-served RemotePilot with top-k, PyTorch, 40-step lines), which #148 tested only for k=1 replay and line errors, never for score parity against #147. Analysis section 9 records that scr-jsearch479 used that path unvalidated, so the rerun carries new information, and the kill rule gates later use on it. This is not the ONNX/PyTorch parity check that H02 lists as do-not-repeat: that check covered the greedy pilot's outputs, and this one covers the whole searched game. Two other arms are also new. The equal-budget breadth-vs-determinization split (k8 d2, k16 d1 at 16 lines) was never run: only k 4/8 at dets 4 on puzzles (#96) and horizons 1/2 (#147) were varied. Test-retest self-agreement of searched choices under independent master seeds is a new readout; #103-106 measured search-vs-pilot disagreement, not search-vs-itself. One minor inaccuracy: distinct_from says '8-16 determinizations at k 8 were never run', but the candidate does not run them either; that H22 untested variant stays open. The candidate does not repeat the verdict question #147 settled (search alone does not flip the walls); it measures how much of search's move is re-deal noise, which the ledger never tested. Rules check passes: play-time search over legal options only, with human lists as evaluation probes.

The re-deal-noise half is diagnostic and matched to its node. Running self-agreement under two independent master seeds, independent versus CRN, on 2,000 fixed positions is a decision-level readout of search noise (N2/N4). Re-deal noise and CRN-null predict clearly different values (independent agreement <=0.65 vs >=0.80; off-top drop >=25% vs <10%). At about 0.01 SE per position metric, those gaps are many SE wide. This part is worth running and is cheap (no screen slot).

The parity half (Same-judge vs Different-judge) is badly calibrated and mostly non-diagnostic as written:

(1) The figures are misstated. #147's one-turn both-sides result is 0.573 with CI [0.469, 0.677], i.e. +/-0.10, not +/-0.07. A fresh 192-game GPU arm has the same CI. Search RNG differs between the two runs, so the difference is barely paired even on identical deals: SE about 0.07. The "> 0.10 off" kill rule is therefore about 1.4 SE. It gives roughly a 15-20% false alarm rate on an identical judge and roughly 50% power against a real 0.10 shift. A 0.05 discrepancy, which would matter, passes silently.

(2) The changed-share bands do not separate the rivals. The GPU path already measured 0.50-0.54 (scr-jsearch479) and 0.533 (smoke), so Same-judge's 0.50-0.56 is already observed and tells nothing about the CPU path. The Different-judge band (outside 0.45-0.60) overlaps it, and the 0.45-0.50 and 0.56-0.60 ranges are assigned to neither rival.

The judges can be compared exactly instead: CPU-ONNX psearch and the GPU-served RemotePilot on the same positions with the same master seed. The only intended differences are numerics, top-k tie order and step caps, so decision agreement should be near 1. Two baselines set the tolerance: CPU-vs-CPU same seed (should be 1.0) and GPU-vs-GPU same seed. GPU batch composition differs run to run, so float nondeterminism can flip near-ties, which is itself a Different-judge mechanism.

The CRN arm's game-score readout is below the stated resolution. The proposal's own paired SE is about 0.04 at 192 games, so neither the prediction that (b) moves the walls >= 0.03 nor the kill clause "nor the score by 0.03" can resolve. The predicted direction ("downward expected") has no stated mechanism.

CRN-null is confounded with an implementation failure. clone(new Rng(seed)) shares the hidden deal across options. But the stream position diverges after different first actions, so later draws may not be coupled. CRN that does not actually couple the worlds would look exactly like CRN-null. A manipulation check is needed.

Smaller issues:
- The puzzle tolerance of +/-2 points has no stated noise.
- The 2,000 positions are drawn from games, so the SE needs clustering by game, or a cap of 1-2 positions per game.
- Agreement is restricted to >=3 options, while off-top/changed share use all >=2-option decisions. The thresholds mix denominators.
- k8 d2 versus k4 d4 at "equal lines" is not equal where there are fewer than 8 legal options; report lines actually spent.
- The kill rules involve no training, so short-horizon bias does not apply. "Keep current search if independent agreement >= 0.85" is sensible.
required_changes: Replace the score-band parity test (0.573 +/- 0.07, kill at > 0.10) with a paired decision-level parity test. On the same >= 500 positions with the same master seed and k4 d4 independent, run CPU-ONNX psearch (walls_vs_humans.js path) against the GPU-served RemotePilot. Report action agreement, plus value correlation on lines from identical clones. Set the tolerance with two baselines: a CPU-vs-CPU same-seed rerun (expect 1.0) and a GPU-vs-GPU same-seed rerun (batch-composition nondeterminism). Different-judge is confirmed if CPU-GPU agreement falls more than 2 SE below GPU-GPU agreement, or if capped or line-error rates differ.

If the 192-game score comparison is kept, correct #147's band to its actual CI [0.469, 0.677] (+/-0.10). State that the comparison with #147 is unpaired at about 0.07 SE and use it as a gross sanity check only, e.g. flag at > 0.15. Use the CPU-run changed share on the same deals as the comparison, not scr-jsearch479's GPU figure.

Remove the 'walls' score moves >= 0.03' prediction and the 0.03 score clause from the CRN kill rule. Either base the CRN decision only on position-level agreement and off-top metrics, or run (a) vs (b) on all 576 deals with the same master seeds and greedy-replay control variates, and state the resulting paired SE. Drop the unexplained 'downward expected' direction, or give a mechanism for it.

Add a CRN manipulation check: for each CRN determinization, the correlation of line scores across the k options. It should be clearly positive and higher than under independent re-deals. Also report the share of lines whose engine RNG stream stays aligned past the first action. CRN-null is interpretable only if this check passes.

Assign the gap between rivals: say what independent self-agreement in 0.65-0.80, or an off-top drop of 10-25%, means (e.g. partial re-deal noise, proceed to C37 only if CRN reaches >= 0.80). Use one denominator (decisions with >= 3 legal options among the top k) for agreement, off-top and changed share alike.

Report position-level SEs clustered by game, or cap positions at 1-2 per game. State the noise of C10's per-class puzzles (e.g. from the two independent master seeds) before using +/-2 points as a threshold.
Report the lines actually spent per decision for k8 d2, k4 d4 and k16 d1, and compare them at matched realized lines (or per option).

reviews.reasons:
Rules: passes. Play-time search over legal options with seeded clones is game-agnostic. CRN only needs an engine that clones and re-deals with a seed, as Game.clone(new Rng(s), viewer) does. Human lists and human-vs-human positions are used for evaluation only. No training input, bot or card-specific term is added.

Engineering: Validation A is cheap and mostly exists already.
- env/remote_worker.js already runs jobs flagged `search` under cmd.judgeSearch {k, dets, maxSteps, concurrency, seed} in a second Runner, and returns searchStats (searches, changed, lines, lineErrors, capped, seconds).
- rl/remote.py already serves topk.
- rl/gpu_matrix.py GpuMatrix.play already sends 'games' messages with raw job seeds. It needs only a judgeSearch passthrough, per-job search flags and the searchStats return, about 30 lines.
- walls_vs_humans.js uses the same SEED*1000003 + p*STRIDE + g seed form, so #147's deals can be reproduced by passing explicit job seeds.
- CRN in PolicySearchAgent is genuinely small. At env/agents.js:377-380, draw one seed per r outside the `for (const a of cands)` loop instead of this.rng.u32() per (a, r): under 10 lines plus an option flag. It is valid CRN: the hidden re-deal happens at clone time, before the option is played, so every option sees the same deal (later shuffles and coin flips diverge, which is acceptable).
- tsearch is a separate path (remote_worker.js:266+, its own probe and lines loop, not reached through judgeSearch), so its CRN is a separate edit.

Underestimated: Validation B.
- No command searches stored positions. It needs a new remote_worker command modelled on tsearch's onDecision probe. That command samples main-phase decisions during greedy games, clones them (clone(new Rng(1))), runs PolicySearchAgent.searchAll under 4 configurations, each twice with independent seeds, and records the chosen action and per-option means. It also needs a Python driver and the analysis.
- It depends on two other candidates' artifacts: C10's per-class puzzles and C01's per-turn Prizes. If those are not built, this candidate owns that work or must drop them.
- Realistic code cost is 6-8 h with tests, not 3-4 h.

Compute:
- 1.6 s a game comes from scr-jsearch479's population games under --max-turns 60. #147's walls-vs-human games have no turn limit, and the walls' deck-out wins have a median of 66 turns, so expect 2-4 s a game. Three 192-game arms take about 20-40 min; the 576-deal extension of all arms takes 1-2 h.
- Positions: 2,500 positions x 8 runs x up to 16 lines is about 320k lines, not 256k, or roughly 9-10 min at #106's rate.
- "No screen slot" is optimistic. The GPU learner adds about 1.5-2 GB to three screens' ~10.5 GB, which sits at the 12.8 GB (80%) cap, and the node workers compete for the 16-thread CPU budget. Run it when at most 2 screens are live, or count it as a slot.

Statistics: the Different-judge test is weak as written.
- #147's own 95% CI for 0.573 is [0.469, 0.677], a half-width of about 0.10, not +/-0.07.
- Two independent 192-game estimates differ with SD about 0.075, so a 0.10 threshold raises a false alarm about 18% of the time and misses real discrepancies below about 0.15.
- A far sharper parity test is cheap: run the CPU-ONNX PolicySearchAgent (walls_vs_humans.js psearch) and the GPU RemotePilot path on the same positions with the same search seed. Compare the decision agreement and the pilot's top-k sets directly. It should be about 1.0 apart from near-ties and fp numerics, and a few hundred positions settle it.
- The changed-share check (SE < 0.005) is also stronger than the score check. The parity decision should rest on these, with the game score secondary.

Value is real. It settles whether the in-loop judge is the one #147 measured, it gives the cheap searched-game infrastructure that C12, C13, C16, C20 and C38 need, and the CRN question has never been asked (H22 and H11 untested).
required_changes: Re-cost the code at 6-8 h. Validation B needs a new remote_worker position-probe command (sample, clone, run each configuration twice with independent seeds, record choices and per-option means), a Python driver and tests. C10's puzzles and C01's per-turn Prizes are external dependencies: either include their cost or make them optional readouts that are dropped if those candidates are not built.

Re-cost the compute. Walls-vs-human searched games without a turn limit run longer than scr-jsearch479's 60-turn-capped games (assume 2-4 s a game: about 20-40 min for the 3 arms, 1-2 h for the 576-deal extension). Positions come to about 320k lines (2,500 positions x 8 runs x <=16 lines), roughly 10 min. Do not claim 'no screen slot': run it with at most 2 screens live, or count it as a slot, because GPU memory (3 x 3.5 GB plus the learner) hits the 12.8 GB cap and node workers share the 16-thread budget.

Replace the score-only parity test with a decision-level parity test. Run the same few hundred positions through the CPU-ONNX PolicySearchAgent (walls_vs_humans.js psearch, resetcap499.onnx) and the GPU RemotePilot path with identical search seeds, and compare top-k sets and chosen actions (expect about 1.0 apart from near-ties). Make the 0.10 game-score threshold secondary. #147's 95% CI half-width is about 0.10, not 0.07, so an unpaired 192-vs-192 comparison at 0.10 raises false alarms about 18% of the time. Fix the noise_and_power numbers to match.

Match #147 exactly in arm (a): maxTurns 0 (no turn limit), maxSteps 40, horizon 1, both seats searched. Reproduce #147's job seeds with walls_vs_humans.js's SEED*1000003 + p*STRIDE + g (seed 11, stride 32, p indexed over the full human list) and the same seat rule, so the deals are paired with #147's rows.

Make adoption of CRN in the in-loop judge or in EI v4's targets rest only on the human-free population positions and games. Report the human-vs-human positions as evaluation diagnostics, never as the gate for a training-side change.

State that tsearch CRN (expert-iteration targets) is a separate edit in remote_worker.js tsearch's line loop, not reached through judgeSearch, and put its tests in env/tools/test_search.js alongside the PolicySearchAgent CRN tests.

title: Named recipe registry, then a bare-versus-stacked delta-debug of the incumbent gate recipe
rivals: H-inert-stack: the stacked flags every gate arm carries (floor 3, group changes 0.3, practice 250, type cap 0.5 with turnover every 5, wide turnover, protect 20) do nothing at the gate's state, so the method can drop them
H-load-bearing: some hold shape or slow the walls (e.g. practice and the varied field keeping the pilot general, #137)
design: (a) Registry: notes/recipes.json (or rl/recipes.py) with fully resolved, non-inheriting named recipes ('adopted-bare', 'gate', 'gate479-stack', 'scratch-factorial-base', later 'stage3'), each flag with value, source log entry and status (adopted / diagnostic / untested / refuted / inert). screen.py --recipe NAME builds the command, rejects duplicate flags (gate479's command passes --turnover-every twice, 10 then 5), and writes resolved flags, the diff from the recipe, hypothesis, rivals, predicted bands and kill rule into screen.jsonl. rl.metagame warns when a resolved flag equals a pre-adoption argparse default not set by a recipe (swaps 3, draft-margin 0.5, lr 1e-4, draft-lr 1e-3, epochs 3, shaping 0). A pre-launch check prints the 3 nearest past screens by flag overlap and the ledger families of changed flags, and requires a stated never-varied factor. (b) First use: 'gate-bare' from scr-resetcap/population_it0479.pt, --reseed 2 (matched to scr-gate479): adopted-bare + --select --candidates 1 --select-z 1 only, 20 iterations. If it differs beyond the A/A band, bisect once: {practice, cap + every 5} vs {floor, group, wide turnover + protect}; a 2^(4-1) fractional factorial in a fresh-start regime follows if two levers interact.

predictions.predicted: gate-bare within the A/A band of scr-gate479: window-mean distance 490-499 within 5 cards, largest type within 15 decks, wall-core decks at 499 within 10, moves within +/-5 an iteration
a difference beyond 2x the A/A band on any of them; under #137's reading, faster type growth and a higher final-pilot walls verdict without practice and the varied field

readout: gate-bare vs scr-gate479: window-mean distance, largest type, wall-core decks, moves, acc-prop, final-pilot walls verdict (C07 protocol); iteration time and RAM without 250 practice games.
noise_and_power: One run against one: only differences above about 5 cards or 15 decks are readable (distance A/A RMS 2.6 from ctl479/resetcap; C29 tightens it). Seven flags drop at once, so a null is strong evidence for pruning and a difference only says where to bisect.
kill_rule: Stop gate-bare at 490 if its wall-core decks exceed scr-gate479's at the same iteration by > 20 (clearly load-bearing); then bisect.
cost: Registry, launcher and checks about 3-4 h of code; gate-bare 20 iterations x about 4.7 min, about 1.6 slot-hours.
distinct_from: The critic's clutter items (stacked-recipe provenance, argparse defaults, duplicate flags) and methodology idea 7's stacking cap. No --select-z run ever dropped the resetcap stack (H25's do-not-repeat lists only stacked variants); H32's verifier asks for the floor/no-floor ablation killed at 453 (one bisection branch here); practice (H16) and turnover (H40) were never isolated under the gate.
rules_check: No method change beyond removing knobs; supports rule 3 and Stage 3's need for one frozen recipe that runs unchanged on Worlds 2005 and MTG.
value: Makes every later screen reproducible and auditable, stops hand-launched runs silently using pre-adoption settings, and either prunes six knobs from the Stage 3 recipe or names the one that carries the effect.
